351.title: Seeing it is seeing
351.hook: whoever sees dependent origination sees the dhamma (MN 28)
351.carry: the seeing is the real thing
351.howItsDone: Buddhist teachers often pair the line from MN 28 with the Buddha's words to Vakkali to explain that the teaching, not the teacher's body, is what students are meant to see.

segments.voice: Yesterday: vedana, feeling, and the seam between the first arrow and the second. Your line: cut between.

A monk named Vakkali lies gravely ill in a potter's shed. Tradition says he had loved the Buddha so much that he followed him around just to look at his face. Now the Buddha comes to his bedside, and Vakkali stirs, trying to get up. For a long time, he says, he'd wanted to come and see the Blessed One, but his body hadn't let him. The Buddha's answer turns what seeing means inside out.
screen: `VAKKALI, GRAVELY ILL.` → `A BEDSIDE VISIT.` → `WHAT SEEING MEANS.`

segments.voice: Here's what the Buddha told Vakkali, in the Connected Discourses. Enough, Vakkali. Why do you want to see this rotting body? Whoever sees the Dhamma sees me; whoever sees me sees the Dhamma. It isn't cold. It's a gift: you don't need my face; you need what I've been pointing at. Now go back to the very first day of this block, the elephant's footprint, Sariputta's great talk in the Middle-Length Discourses. Near its end, after walking through the body's elements and the five heaps, Sariputta quotes the Buddha with a line of the same shape. Whoever sees dependent origination sees the Dhamma. Whoever sees the Dhamma sees dependent origination. Put the two together. To see the Buddha is to see the Dhamma. To see the Dhamma is to see dependent arising: this, because of that. So in these two suttas, the seeing that counts isn't of a person or a place or a vision. It's seeing how things lean on each other. How a mood leans on sleep. How craving leans on feeling. How dukkha leans on craving, and ends when craving ends. Sariputta draws the conclusion right there in the sutta: the five heaps are dependently arisen, and the desire and clinging for them is the origin of dukkha. Seeing it isn't a step before the real thing. The seeing is the real thing.

352.title: The truths, closed
352.hook: four truths, three turns, twelve links
352.howItsDone: Buddhist schools teach the four noble truths as a core of the Dhamma; in Theravada communities the first sermon, which sets them out, is often chanted in Pali, notably on the full moon of Asalha.

segments.voice: Yesterday: dhamma. Whoever sees dependent arising sees the Dhamma. Your line: the seeing is the real thing.

segments.voice: At the end of a long hike, some people turn around at the trailhead and look back up at the mountain. From down here it looks small, a single shape against the sky. But the hiker remembers every switchback: where the path got steep, where they sat on a rock, where the view opened. Three weeks ago, year two began at an elephant's footprint, with Sariputta saying that every wholesome thing fits inside four truths. Today, a look back up at those four, before the path turns toward the eight.
screen: `LOOKING BACK UP THE MOUNTAIN.` → `EVERY SWITCHBACK.` → `FOUR TRUTHS, BEFORE THE EIGHT.`

segments.voice: Here's the whole block. The elephant's footprint, the print that holds all others, and a physician's pattern: illness, cause, cure, treatment. The first truth in full: birth, aging, sickness, death, not getting what you want. Three kinds of dukkha: pain, change, and the unease of made things. Its task: to be understood. The second truth, samudaya, three thirsts, and its task: to be let go, like a wish that ends at the park. The third, nirodha: it can stop, the burden set down. Nibbana, the fire gone out. Its task: to be realized, tasted like the ocean's salt. The fourth, magga, the eightfold path, and its task: to be developed, walked into being. Three turns and twelve aspects: the Buddha's own checklist before he claimed awakening. A handful of leaves: only what helps. Salla: treat the wound first. Kacchapa: a rare life, so look into the truths. And underneath it all, paticcasamuppada, this because of that, laid out in twelve links, with a seam between feeling and craving where the chain can break. Seeing that is seeing the Dhamma. The Dhammapada, in Max Müller's translation, gathers the four truths into a single line: "pain, the origin of pain, the destruction of pain, and the eightfold holy way that leads to the quieting of pain." One way to read the list: three of the four truths are set up for the last one. Understand, let go, realize: all of it gets done by walking. Block B takes the eightfold path one factor at a time, starting tomorrow with how the eight fit together.

353.title: Eight spokes, one wheel
353.hook: the eight factors in three trainings: wisdom, conduct, meditation (MN 44)
353.howItsDone: Buddhist teachers commonly teach the eightfold path through the three trainings of conduct, meditation and wisdom, and the eight-spoked dharma wheel appears on temples, flags and books across Asia.

segments.voice: Yesterday: the truths, closed. Four truths, each with its task, resting on dependent arising. Your line: four truths, one path.

The commentaries tell the backstory. A merchant named Visakha comes home from hearing the Buddha teach, changed for good, and his wife, Dhammadinna, notices. Soon she goes forth as a nun, practices hard, and, tradition says, becomes fully awakened. One day Visakha visits her and, instead of small talk, asks her question after question about the teaching. She answers every one. When he reports the conversation to the Buddha, the Buddha says he would have answered exactly the same way.
screen: `VISAKHA'S WIFE BECOMES A NUN.` → `QUESTION AFTER QUESTION.` → `I'D HAVE ANSWERED THE SAME.`

segments.voice: The conversation is in the Middle-Length Discourses, number forty-four. One of Visakha's questions is about how the path fits together: are the three trainings included in the noble eightfold path, or is the path included in the three trainings? Dhammadinna answers that the eight are sorted into the three. Right speech, right action and right livelihood belong to conduct, sila: how you live with others. Right effort, right mindfulness and right concentration belong to meditation, samadhi: how you train the mind. Right view and right intention belong to wisdom, panna: how you see, and what you aim for. Eight factors, three trainings. Now the wheel. The dharma wheel with eight spokes is a later symbol, carved and painted all over Asia, on temple gates and flags. But it fits her answer. A wheel with a missing spoke still turns, badly. A wheel with all eight runs true. And no spoke comes first: they all meet at the hub and touch the rim at once. The path's own list starts with right view, so some teachers say wisdom comes first: you need a view to start walking. Dhammadinna names conduct first, so others say a calm, honest life is the ground for everything else. Both orders are in the texts. What they agree on is that the three trainings lean on each other, like the spokes. Over the next weeks, we'll take each spoke on its own, starting tomorrow with right view. And remember who drew this map: a nun, whose answers the Buddha said he would have given himself.

354.title: Right view
354.hook: knowing dukkha, its arising, its ending, and the way (MN 9)
354.howItsDone: The Sammaditthi Sutta, Sariputta's talk on right view, is studied in Theravada monasteries, and teachers in several schools describe right view as seeing through the lens of the four truths.

segments.voice: Yesterday: eight spokes, sorted by the nun Dhammadinna into conduct, meditation and wisdom. Your line: all meet at the hub.
screen: `EIGHT SPOKES — ALL MEET AT THE HUB.`

segments.voice: Put on someone else's glasses and the world tilts. The edges blur, the floor seems closer, you reach for a cup and miss. Nothing in the room changed. Only the lens did. Right view, the first factor of the eightfold path, is about the lens. And a long explanation of it comes not from the Buddha but from Sariputta again, in a talk where the monks keep asking, politely, for more. Each time, he finds another way to say it.
screen: `SOMEONE ELSE'S GLASSES.` → `ONLY THE LENS CHANGED.` → `THE MONKS KEEP ASKING.`

segments.voice: The Pali is samma ditthi. Ditthi means view: a way of seeing. Samma, as we've heard, means right, complete, fitting. The talk is the ninth in the Middle-Length Discourses. Sariputta asks: in what way is a disciple of right view, whose view is straight? The monks ask him to explain, and he does it in a pattern he repeats again and again. When someone understands the unwholesome and its root, the wholesome and its root, that is right view. Good, friend, say the monks, but might there be another way? Yes, he says, and explains it through food and nourishment. Then through the four truths: understanding dukkha, its arising, its ending, and the way to its ending. Then through each of the twelve links: aging and death, its arising, its ending, the way. Around and around, the same four-part shape. So right view here isn't mainly a set of opinions to sign. It's a way of looking at anything: what is this, where does it come from, can it end, and how? Another sutta in the Connected Discourses, defining all eight factors, gives the short form: right view is knowledge of dukkha, its arising, its ending, and the way. That's the lens. The four truths aren't only a teaching to remember. They're also glasses to see through. A bad night's sleep, a fight with a sibling, a fear about money: each can be looked at the same four ways. For Sariputta, that's what makes a view right: it looks at anything in terms of where it comes from and how it ends.

355.title: Roots
355.hook: Sariputta: the roots of the unwholesome are greed, hate and delusion; their opposites are the wholesome roots (MN 9)
355.howItsDone: Buddhist teaching across schools names the three unwholesome roots, greed, hatred and delusion, and the ten courses of action; some practitioners reflect at the end of the day on which roots their actions came from.

segments.voice: Yesterday: samma ditthi, right view, the four truths used as a lens. Your line: see it as it is.

segments.voice: Anyone who's pulled weeds knows the trick. Snap off the top and you've done nothing; next week it's back, greener than before. You have to get your fingers down into the soil and ease out the root, the pale stringy part you never see. Sariputta's first answer in his talk on right view is about exactly this. Before the four truths, before the twelve links, he starts with actions and the roots they grow from.
screen: `SNAP OFF THE TOP.` → `IT'S BACK NEXT WEEK.` → `EASE OUT THE ROOT.`

segments.voice: Kusala is usually translated wholesome, or skillful. In everyday Pali it can describe someone skilled at a craft, or someone well and healthy. Its opposite is akusala: unwholesome, unskillful. Sariputta begins by naming ten unwholesome actions, a list later called the ten unwholesome courses of action: killing, stealing, sexual misconduct, lying, divisive speech, harsh speech, idle chatter, covetousness, ill will and wrong view. Three of the body, four of speech, three of the mind. Then the roots. What is the root of the unwholesome? Greed is a root. Hatred is a root. Delusion is a root. And the wholesome? Abstaining from those ten. And its roots: non-greed, non-hatred, non-delusion. Sariputta doesn't stop at the list of actions. The ten are the weeds above the ground; the roots are what keep them coming back. You can stop lying for a week by force of will, but if the greed or fear underneath is untouched, the lie grows back. The wholesome roots are described with a not, but some teachers explain them positively as well: non-greed shows up as generosity, non-hatred as kindness, non-delusion as wisdom. So a single generous act isn't only a nice thing done. It's a root being watered. And why does Sariputta start here, in a talk about right view? Seeing clearly begins with seeing what's actually driving what you do. Not to feel guilty about it. To know which root to tend.

356.title: Worldly right view
356.hook: that giving bears fruit, that deeds matter, that there are good teachers (MN 117)
356.howItsDone: In Theravada lay practice, right view is often lived as confidence in kamma: giving to monks and the needy, honoring parents and teachers, and trusting that good actions bear good fruit.

segments.voice: Yesterday: kusala, the wholesome, growing from non-greed, non-hatred and non-delusion. Your line: a root being watered.

Six in the morning, a village road, and a grandmother who has never read a sutta is already waiting with a pot of rice for the monks' bowls. She does this every day. She's honest at the market. She tells her grandchildren that what you do comes back to you, that your parents deserve respect, that there are good people in the world worth listening to. Does she have right view, or is that only for scholars who can recite the twelve links? The Buddha says there are two kinds of right view. She has the first.
screen: `A GRANDMOTHER WHO NEVER READ A SUTTA.` → `RICE, HONESTY, RESPECT.` → `TWO KINDS OF RIGHT VIEW.`

segments.voice: The sutta is number one hundred seventeen in the Middle-Length Discourses, the Great Forty. In it the Buddha says right view is twofold. There's right view still bound up with the world, sharing in merit and ripening in good results. And there's right view that is noble, beyond the world: the wisdom of someone who has entered the path for real. Then he spells out the worldly kind, as things a person holds to be so. There is what is given: giving bears fruit. There is fruit and result of good and bad deeds. There is this world and the other world. There is mother and father, which the commentaries read as: they matter, and are owed gratitude. There are beings reborn spontaneously. And there are good, well-practiced teachers who have seen these things for themselves and make them known. Not complicated philosophy: basic confidence that actions have consequences, that generosity isn't wasted, that parents and teachers count. In Pali, the action is kamma, karma in Sanskrit, and its result is vipaka, the ripening. The Buddha doesn't call worldly right view second-rate; teachers often describe it as the ground the noble kind grows from. And again and again in the same sutta he says right view comes first, because it lets you tell wrong view as wrong and right view as right. So the grandmother with her rice pot isn't doing something less than the scholar. She's on the first floor of the same house. Modern Buddhists hold different views about rebirth and other worlds, and teachers address that in different ways. The list's center holds across them: deeds matter.

Your line: deeds matter. Small kindnesses ripen in places you may never see. See you tomorrow.

357.title: Stoics and Buddhists
357.hook: two calm schools that get mixed up online: what's in our power (Epictetus) and the second arrow (SN 36.6); similar practice, different reasons
357.tomorrow: the blind men and the elephant
357.howItsDone: Buddhist teachers who are asked about Stoicism often point to shared practices, watching reactions and reflecting on death, while noting that Buddhism grounds them in impermanence and not-self rather than in a reasoned cosmic order.

segments.voice: Yesterday: vipaka, and your line, deeds matter. Giving bears fruit, and kamma ripens. Day three hundred fifty-seven.

Two lines on a poster. One says it isn't things that upset us, but our opinions about them. The other says pain is one arrow, and we fire a second one into ourselves. Which one is the Buddha? Online, they sometimes get swapped. The first is Epictetus, a Greek teacher who had once been enslaved in the Roman empire. The second is the Buddha, in paraphrase. People keep asking whether Stoicism and Buddhism are the same thing. To close the right view week, an honest look.
screen: `TWO LINES ON A POSTER.` → `WHICH ONE IS THE BUDDHA?` → `THE SAME THING?`

segments.voice: Start with what's alike. Epictetus begins his handbook, in George Long's translation: "Of things some are in our power, and others are not." Our judgments, our wanting and not wanting, are ours. The body, money, reputation, are not. Train yourself to tell the difference, and much of the distress falls away. The Buddha's second arrow works the same ground. Someone untrained, struck by pain, adds worry and resistance on top: two arrows. Someone trained feels the first and doesn't fire the second. Both schools watch their reactions closely. Both reflect on death on purpose. Both prize a steady mind. That's why the comparison keeps coming up. Now the difference, and it's in the reasons. The Stoics taught that the world is ordered by a divine reason, the logos, and the good life is living in agreement with it. Virtue, they said, is the only true good, and your reasoning mind is the part that is really yours. The Buddha's teaching doesn't rest on a cosmic order. It looks at what arises and passes, and turns the same look on the one doing the judging: is this me, is this mine? Its aim isn't agreement with nature. It's the end of craving. Same calm on the surface, different roots underneath. Neither needs the other to be wrong. And this week has been about exactly that: right view as a lens, not a trophy. Seeing it is seeing, the truths closed, eight spokes, right view, roots, deeds that ripen, and today, two schools side by side.
screen: `WHAT'S IN OUR POWER, AND WHAT ISN'T.` · `ONE ARROW, NOT TWO.` · `A REASONED COSMOS, OR NOT-SELF.` · `SAME CALM, DIFFERENT ROOTS.` · then, large: `SAME CALM, DIFFERENT REASONS.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind something small that's bothering you today. First, the Buddha's question: what is the first arrow here, the thing that actually happened, and what is the second, the part the mind keeps adding? Then Epictetus's question: what here is in my power, and what isn't? Notice which question loosens something in you; there's no right answer, so just rest with the breath.
Stoicism. A Greek and Roman philosophy of calm through clear judgment: a neighbor to this path, with a similar practice and different reasons. Today's word.
Your line: same calm, different reasons. Two schools can look alike and still be two schools. Day three hundred fifty-seven.
